I decided to collect photographers’ portfolios to create this tribute album after I heard about the death of my friend Gideon Pauker from Kibbutz Nir Oz on what has become to be called “the Black Sabbath” of October 2023. October 7th was the date of my return flight to Israel, but my flight was cancelled like all the others. Until I could find an alternative flight, I spent an entire week wandering around the canals of Amsterdam, consumed with worry, pain, and distress. I was unable to understand how so many good people were gone in one fell swoop. I chose to upload the photographers’ portfolios to my Facebook page accompanied by the hashtag #Album Darom: Israeli photographers in tribute to the residents of the Western Negev. It was important to me to begin with photographers who reside in the area. On October 20, 2023, I published my first post. I embarked on the project equipped with two dozen portfolios from photographers who were going to collaborate with me. The initial list comprised photographers whom I love and admire who agreed to contribute work. Each day I posted one photographer’s pictures, and as the number of participants gradually increased, the tribute continued for over one hundred days. This “state of emergency routine” in which I posted daily at a set time every day was a tremendous comfort to me. (Only once, when I returned home late from the North did I postpone the post to 11 p.m.). In a parallel and fascinating process in and of itself, I made the decision to allow Album Darom to live beyond Facebook and initiate its publication as a book and museum exhibitions. The exhibition at the Petach Tikva Museum of Art (June 2024) will be followed by one at the Yad Mordechai Museum (October 2024). The decision to publish was made despite the full realization that it is too soon for a fully developed historical perspective. Album Darom captures the experiences of people who have lost those dearest to them. They unveil an unprecedented chapter in the history of the State of Israel, the full implications of which are still unfolding. The poignant human narratives that emerge from the pages of the album are recounted by the photographers themselves. In addition to the visual evidence, the book also contains written testimonies of the events of October 7th, such as texts by Shahar Vahab (p.224) or Sholi Strauss (p.130). The story of the youngest participant, the late Lavi Lipshitz z”l, a combat soldier in the Givati commando unit who fell in battle on October 31, 2023, is recounted by his mother Shlomit. On the morning of October 7th, when complete shock still prevailed, and certainly afterwards, when the intensity of the event became clear, press, army, and police photographers, along with others, took tremendous risks and traveled south with media teams or independently. They stood speechless in the face of the enormous destruction, yet carefully documented the events, providing a vivid picture of the disaster. Sometimes press photographers find themselves deep in horrifying situations, as do police photographers, those who work with ZAKA Search and Rescue who identify remains, and others. Trauma leaves traces on those who are exposed to it, and its impact warrants methodical research, certainly in Israel. I have devoted the epilogue of Album Darom to a photographed essay entitled ”Being Lee Miller: From ’Zionist Phantom’ to ’Coal Scars” (See pp. 254–278 in Hebrew). The essay deals with trauma and its appearances in the Western Negev. This landscape is full with relics that appear in this area of continues disaster. My creation deals with the remains of the conflict and the results of the military operations. The work on this series of photos started in 2017 and lasted until the opening of my solo exhibition ”Coal Scars” in October 2021, in the Yad Mordechai Museum in the Negev. Senior press photographers may perhaps choose which story to shoot, but they do not have the privilege of deciding not to go out into the field as do art photographers. The urgency to document a disaster drives the work of photojournalism but does not apply to art photographers, nor to painters, sculptors, illustrators, designers, animators, and filmmakers. They can choose whether or not to express traumatic events in their art, some making works in response to trauma decades after the events. In the first decade of the twentieth century, leading photographers documented Kinneret, Degania and Kfar Giladi; in the 1920s they documented Ein Harod and the Jezreel Valley settlements; in the 1930s, stockade-and-tower settlements including Hanita, Nir David and Negba; and from the 1940s, the new frontier settlements in the western Negev, including the eleven points, among them Be’eri and Nirim, established in 1946. After the state was founded, with the establishment of the Nahal, settlement expanded across the country. The first Nahal outpost was established at Nahal Oz in 1951.
